strengths: Addresses a real and previously unexplored gap: integrating watermark embedding with anchor-based 3DGS compression (HAC/ContextGS), which is a practically relevant problem given commercial deployment of 3DGS.

The quantization distortion layer (QDL) is a simple but effective mechanism that yields dramatically better post-compression bit accuracy (e.g., 95.92% vs. 54.40% for HAC+WateRF in Table 1), and its benefit is isolated in a dedicated ablation (Table 7).

Comprehensive experimental design: three standard datasets (Blender, LLFF, Mip-NeRF 360), two compression backends, multiple message lengths (32/48/64 bits), six image distortions, and three model distortions, covering fidelity, robustness, and capacity.

Useful ablations beyond the main components, including a study of which anchor attribute to embed the watermark in (Table 6), which supports the design choice of the anchor feature over position/scaling/offsets.

The proposed learnable watermark embedding feature (Eq. 5) is a clean, low-overhead way to inject the message into anchor features without altering the model architecture, and the frequency-aware anchor growing mechanism is a plausible remedy for quality degradation.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core robustness mechanism (adding uniform noise to simulate quantization during training) is a well-established technique from learned image compression and HiDDeN-style watermarking; the contribution is largely an adaptation/integration of known ideas to anchor-based 3DGS rather than a new technical insight.

Fairness of baseline comparisons is questionable. The baselines (WateRF, GaussianMarker, 3D-GSW) were not designed for quantization-based anchor compression and appear to be evaluated without an equivalent adaptation or distortion-aware training, so their drastic post-compression drops may partly reflect misapplication rather than intrinsic weakness of the watermarking methods themselves.

Reliance on a frozen, pre-trained HiDDeN decoder applied to a one-level DWT LL subband is under-analyzed: the paper does not explain why a decoder trained on natural images works well on LL subbands, nor discuss implications of a fixed decoder for security (the message space and decoder are publicly known).

Reporting inconsistencies and clarity issues reduce confidence: Table 4 cites GaussianMarker and 3D-GSW with reference [10] (WateRF); Table 1 pre-compression sizes (e.g., 208 MB for HAC+CompMarkGS) are not explained or contextualized; several typos ('Guassians', 'Wateramrk', 'dimentional'); Figure 3 contains implausible values (PSNR 6.26) that are not discussed.

Incomplete methodological details for reproducibility: key hyperparameters of the frequency-aware anchor growing (τ, β, K, growing schedule) and anchor growing procedure are deferred to a supplementary that is not provided; no code release is mentioned; test-set details for LLFF/Mip-NeRF 360 are vague (only 200 images specified for Blender).

The frequency-aware anchor growing operates on a per-view 2D high-frequency mask mapped back to 3D anchors, which is inherently view-dependent; the paper does not discuss how multi-view inconsistencies in the mask are handled or whether this creates view-dependent artifacts.

Significance is somewhat bounded: the method requires training the watermarked model end-to-end per scene with a fixed decoder and fixed bit length, and the limitation discussion (pre-trained decoder) is brief; broader applicability (e.g., post-hoc watermarking of already-trained models) is not addressed.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practically relevant gap: no prior 3DGS watermarking method is designed to survive quantization-based model compression, and the problem formulation (joint watermark embedding + compression) is well motivated.

The experimental evaluation is broad: two state-of-the-art compression backbones (HAC, ContextGS), 25 scenes across three standard datasets, six image distortions, three model distortions, and three message capacities (32/48/64 bits), with reasonable baselines (WateRF, GaussianMarker, 3D-GSW).

The headline result is convincing in magnitude: after HAC compression the proposed method retains ~95.9% bit accuracy versus 46-58% for baselines, and PSNR remains essentially unchanged (27.68 -> 27.65), demonstrating that the quantization distortion layer solves the stated failure mode.

Component-wise ablations are provided for the quantization distortion layer (Tab. 7), watermark embedding target (Tab. 6), and the combination of frequency-aware growing and auxiliary losses (Tab. 5), supporting the design choices.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core ingredients are individually well established: quantization-aware training via injected rounding noise (a soft version of the straight-through estimator), frequency-domain watermark embedding following WateRF, a frozen pre-trained HiDDeN decoder, and standard anchor-based compression from Scaffold-GS/HAC/ContextGS. The contribution is largely an engineering combination of existing pieces, and much of the robustness is inherited from the off-the-shelf HiDDeN decoder rather than from a new watermarking principle.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence in the results. The text states 'removing all components improved bit accuracy' but Table 5 shows the full method achieves the highest bit accuracy (95.16 vs 94.68 without FAG). Figure 4 reports identical bit accuracy (97.91) with and without FAG, and only a 0.32 dB PSNR difference, which weakens the claimed benefit of the frequency-aware anchor growing module.

The capacity study (Tab. 4) claims a trade-off where 'degradation of both image quality and bit accuracy' occurs with more bits, but only bit accuracy is reported; no image quality metrics are given for the 32/64-bit settings, so the trade-off claim is unsupported.

Several clarity and correctness issues: 'vanilla 3DGS [11]' cites 3D-GSW rather than the 3DGS paper; Eq. (6) is garbled in notation; 'alpha_i in R^3' in Eq. (2) should be a scalar; typos ('Guassians', 'Wateramrk', 'dimentional', 'Each components'); the epsilon=0.3 mask parameter is introduced loosely and the high-frequency anchor growing procedure is deferred to supplementary material, hurting reproducibility.

The security evaluation is one-sided. Only bit accuracy under random perturbations is measured; there is no analysis of false positive rates, key secrecy, or adaptive/white-box attacks such as model fine-tuning or over-fitting a new decoder, which are the realistic threats for copyright verification. The claim of 'robust' copyright protection is stronger than the evidence.

The motivation for the HSV loss and the frequency loss is thin, and the frequency-aware anchor growing mechanism (Gaussian high-pass mask, median-based pixel selection, hash-matching) reads as a collection of heuristics with limited analysis of sensitivity to hyperparameters (tau, beta, epsilon).

Comparisons may be slightly unfair: 3D-GSW is evaluated after pruning-based preprocessing, and baseline watermarking methods were not designed for the anchor-based compression pipeline; nonetheless, presenting HAC+baseline numbers dropping to 13-14 dB PSNR suggests tuning issues on the baseline side rather than a purely methodological gap.
No discussion of computational overhead (training time increase over Scaffold-GS, decoding cost), and no statement about code release, limiting reproducibility.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important gap: existing 3DGS watermarking methods (GaussianMarker, 3D-GSW, WateRF) are not designed to survive quantization-based model compression, and this appears to be the first work to embed watermarks in anchor-based (Scaffold-GS-style) 3DGS with compression compatibility.

The core idea is sound and well-motivated: simulating quantization noise during training (a quantization distortion layer, QDL) so the model pre-adapts to compression is a natural and effective fix, and Table 7 shows a clear gain (90.75 -> 95.92 bit accuracy after compression with ContextGS).

Comprehensive evaluation: two compression backbones (HAC, ContextGS), three benchmark datasets, three bit lengths, six image distortions, three model distortions, plus ablations on each component (FAG, HSV loss, frequency loss, QDL) and on the choice of embedding target (Table 6), which supports the design decisions.

Results are convincing where they matter most: after compression the method retains ~95% bit accuracy and near-identical PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS (Table 1), while all baselines collapse (e.g., HAC+WateRF drops from 91.02 to 54.40), directly validating the central claim.

The frequency-aware anchor growing mechanism is a reasonably novel contribution that couples the watermarking objective with 3DGS densification, and the analysis of why embedding into position/scaling/offsets degrades quality (Table 6) is informative.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is largely a combination of existing ingredients — HiDDeN's pre-trained decoder, DWT low-frequency embedding (following WateRF), noise-layer simulation of quantization (a well-known trick in deep watermarking), and standard anchor-based compression. The individual components are known; the contribution is primarily their adaptation and integration for 3DGS.

Security analysis is shallow for a watermarking paper: there is no discussion of the secret key, no evaluation against adaptive or deliberate watermark-removal attacks (only generic noise/geometry distortions), and the threat model for 'malicious use' in Fig. 1 is not formally defined. A 48-bit message at ~95% accuracy still leaves room for error-correcting-code discussion that is absent.

Storage overhead is not adequately analyzed: the watermark embedding feature f' is a learnable per-anchor parameter (Table 1 shows HAC+CompMarkGS at 208.96 MB vs. 173.64 MB for 3D-GSW before compression). The paper does not clarify whether f' is itself quantized/entropy-coded during compression, nor report the training-time overhead relative to unwatermarked HAC/ContextGS.

Presentation and reporting issues: Table 4's caption cites [10] for GaussianMarker and 3D-GSW (incorrect references); Table 3 reports model-distortion robustness only 'before quantization compression,' which is an odd and inconsistently motivated evaluation point; typos ('Guassians', 'Wateramrk', 'dimentional').

The quantization distortion layer injects rounding noise, but HAC's actual compression pipeline involves hash-grid quantization plus interpolation and entropy coding, which the authors themselves acknowledge is harder to simulate; the fidelity of the QDL approximation to real compression is not empirically characterized (e.g., behavior under mismatched quantization steps or unseen compressors).

The claimed compression advantage is partly inherited from ContextGS (5.72 MB) rather than the watermarking method itself; a comparison against unwatermarked compressed baselines to quantify the watermarking-specific quality/storage cost would strengthen the claims.
Several implementation details are deferred to supplementary material (anchor growing details, scaffold loss), limiting reproducibility from the main paper alone; no code release is mentioned.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper identifies a genuine, previously unaddressed gap—existing 3DGS watermarking methods fail under quantization-based model compression—and provides the first targeted solution.

Solid core technical idea: embedding the watermark into the anchor feature (rather than directly into Gaussian attributes) and simulating quantization noise during training (QDL) is a sensible and effective design, validated by the largest-ablation component (removing QDL causes the biggest drop in Table 5).

Comprehensive evaluation: two compression schemes (HAC, ContextGS), three datasets, three bit lengths, image-level distortions, model-level attacks (noise, clone, prune), pruning-based compression (LightGaussian), general float32→int8 quantization, PGD attacks, decoder-independence (SSL decoder), FPS, and per-attribute embedding ablations.
Strong empirical results: bit accuracy remains ~95% after compression vs. ~50–60% for baselines under HAC, with comparable or better rendering quality (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) and competitive model size.
Honest discussion of distinctions from related work (SecureGS, 3D-GSW, GuardSplat) and limitations, plus detailed implementation details in the appendix supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty of individual components: the QDL is a straightforward application of the classical differentiable distortion-layer idea (HiDDeN-style noise augmentation) to anchor features, and the frequency-aware anchor growing and HSV loss are largely engineering heuristics; the contribution is primarily a well-engineered combination rather than a new technique.

The main paper lacks an important reference point: rendering quality and bit accuracy of an uncompressed, unwatermarked Scaffold-GS baseline, making it hard to quantify the fidelity cost of watermarking itself.

Baselines require significant re-implementation for the anchor-based setting (especially GuardSplat, whose SH-offset mechanism is fundamentally modified), so the comparison may under-represent what baselines could achieve with principled adaptation; no comparison against SecureGS or GS-Hider is provided.

Robustness is only evaluated against the two specific quantization-based compressors whose quantization noise distribution the QDL was designed to mimic (plus int8); generalization to unseen or future compression methods (e.g., CAT-3DGS, pruning+entropy methods outside the anchor family) is only partially explored.

Security claims (watermark is 'extremely difficult' for an attacker to detect/remove via the MLP indirection) are asserted but never empirically tested with an actual removal or detection attack; ownership-provision aspects such as false-positive rate and key/security analysis are absent.

Some results are under-explained: e.g., ContextGS+CompMarkGS is 73.39 MB before compression versus ~177–342 MB for baselines, a large discrepancy that is not analyzed; Table 9 shows substantial post-quantization PSNR/SSIM degradation (~5 dB) that is not discussed.
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility for a method whose practical value depends on exact training details and thresholds.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely new and practically relevant problem: watermark robustness to quantization-based 3DGS compression, which prior 3DGS watermarking works (GaussianMarker, 3D-GSW, GuardSplat, WateRF) do not handle.

Comprehensive evaluation: three standard datasets (Blender, LLFF, Mip-NeRF 360), two compression schemes (HAC, ContextGS), three message lengths, image- and model-distortion attacks, PGD adversarial attacks, pruning-based compression (LightGaussian), general float32->int8 quantization, decoder-independence (HiDDeN vs SSL decoder), and FPS measurements.
Thorough ablation studies covering embedding location (anchor feature vs. position/scaling/offsets), QDL, FAG, and HSV loss, with post-compression metrics consistently reported.
The method maintains high bit accuracy after compression (e.g., 95.92% under HAC) while preserving rendering quality, a large gap relative to adapted baselines that collapse after compression.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core components are straightforward adaptations of existing ideas: the quantization distortion layer is essentially additive uniform rounding noise during training (a standard distortion-layer/data-augmentation trick from HiDDeN-era watermarking), the frequency-aware anchor growing is error-map-guided densification, and the HSV loss is a minor perceptual-loss variant. The anchor-feature embedding is a natural design choice rather than a conceptual advance.

Baseline fairness concerns. All baselines were re-implemented inside an anchor-based framework, and GuardSplat required substantial architectural modification (offsets applied to anchor features instead of SH coefficients). Reported baseline results (e.g., GuardSplat at ~16 dB PSNR pre-compression) may reflect poor adaptation rather than the true performance of those methods. Moreover, baselines fine-tune pretrained models while CompMarkGS trains from scratch with pruning/growing integrated, making the comparison protocol asymmetric.

The motivation rests partly on claims that are not rigorously substantiated: security through MLP-based indirection is asserted ('extremely difficult for a malicious user to detect or remove') without any formal analysis or removal/detection attack experiments against the anchor-feature embedding itself.

Results for GaussianMarker in Table 12 look anomalous (~58-61% bit accuracy under every distortion, including trivial ones like scaling) and are not explained, raising questions about baseline implementation quality.

Pre-compression model sizes are very large (e.g., ~209 MB for HAC + CompMarkGS, ~341 MB for GaussianMarker variant), and the paper does not report embedding/training time overhead relative to baselines, which weakens the practicality narrative.

The FAG and HSV loss components give relatively small gains (Tab.5: ~1-5% bit accuracy, modest PSNR/LPIPS changes), suggesting they are incremental refinements bundled to strengthen the contribution list rather than independent contributions.

Robustness is only demonstrated for two specific quantization-based compression schemes (HAC, ContextGS); generalization to other compression pipelines (e.g., vector-quantization-only methods like CompGS or LightGaussian pre-quantization) is only partially covered.

strengths: Identifies a genuine and practically important gap: existing 3DGS watermarking methods degrade under quantization-based model compression, and no prior work explicitly addresses this. The problem formulation (watermark robustness to compression as an owner-distribution scenario) is well motivated and timely given the industrial adoption of 3DGS.

The core idea is sensible and well executed: embedding the watermark in the anchor feature of an anchor-based (Scaffold-GS style) representation, so that the watermark passes through non-linear MLPs, plus a quantization distortion layer (QDL) that simulates quantization noise during training. This is a natural and appropriate adaptation of the established differentiable-noise/STE training paradigm to the model-compression setting.

Extensive and mostly convincing evaluation: three standard datasets (Blender, LLFF, Mip-NeRF 360), two compression schemes (HAC and ContextGS), four baselines adapted to the anchor-based setting, message-length sweep (32/48/64 bits), image-distortion and model-distortion robustness, PGD adversarial attacks, decoder-independence check (DINO-based SSL decoder), general int8 quantization, pruning-based compression, FPS measurements, and thorough ablations (Tables 4, 5, 7, 8-13). The post-compression results (e.g., 95.9% vs ~54% bit accuracy under HAC) are striking and support the central claim.

Good ablation coverage: embedding into different anchor attributes (position/scaling/offsets vs. feature), and component-wise ablations showing QDL contributes most to bit accuracy and FAG/HSV loss to rendering quality. The dedicated watermark embedding feature ablation (Table 7) addresses the capacity-confound question.

The paper is well written, with a clear pipeline figure, explicit equations, and a detailed appendix covering implementation, related-work distinctions (e.g., SecureGS steganography vs. watermarking), limitations, and ethics/data provenance.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the building blocks are largely assembled from prior art - the anchor representation from Scaffold-GS, the pre-trained HiDDeN decoder from 2018, uniform quantization noise simulation from HAC and the classic watermarking distortion-layer literature (HiDDeN, Zhu et al.). The contribution is primarily a system-level adaptation to compression robustness rather than a new technique; FAG and the HSV loss are relatively incremental quality-improvement components.

The QDL injects uniform rounding-error-like noise rather than an actual quantizer or straight-through-estimator quantization, and the quantization scale q_i is learnable via MLP_q; the paper does not justify why this approximation faithfully matches real entropy-coding pipelines (which also involve codebooks, arithmetic coding, and anchor-Gaussian interpolation errors). The mechanism that makes the watermark survive HAC's interpolation step, which the paper itself identifies as a 'compounding problem,' is not clearly explained.

Fairness of baseline comparison is a concern: all baselines (WateRF, GaussianMarker, 3D-GSW, GuardSplat) were designed for vanilla 3DGS or NeRF and are re-implemented/adapted to the anchor-based framework, with GuardSplat requiring substantial architectural modification (SH offsets moved to anchor features). The adapted baselines were not optimized for this setting, so the large gaps may partly reflect suboptimal adaptation rather than fundamental method superiority.

The method trains the watermarked anchor-based 3DGS from scratch per scene, whereas several baselines fine-tune pretrained models. This changes the embedding budget and training cost, and makes the comparison of model sizes (Table 1) and training overhead less apples-to-apples; per-scene training cost/runtime and generalization to unseen scenes are not reported.

Capacity remains limited (64 bits) and extraction requires access to the pre-trained decoder; there is no analysis of false-positive rate, multiple-watermark scenarios, or security against watermark-removal attacks specifically tailored to anchor features (beyond PGD on the decoder). The claim of being 'the first compression-robust 3DGS watermarking' is plausible but relies on an exhaustive survey of concurrent work.

Some presentation issues: Eq. 5 and the binary-mask construction in Eq. 11 (selecting pixels within [median-eps, median+eps] of the error) is unintuitive - it selects mid-error pixels rather than the highest-error pixels, and the justification (avoiding outliers) is thin. Figure 4 presents distortion results only as a radar-style summary, with the quantitative detail relegated to the appendix.
